q: Proteins are natural polymers whose monomer units are:
x: Proteins are polyamides built from α-amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Monosaccharides build polysaccharides and nucleotides build nucleic acids.

q: The linkage that joins amino acid units in a protein is:
x: The peptide (amide) linkage –CO–NH– forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. –CO–O– is an ester link and –O– is the glycosidic link of carbohydrates.

q: Formation of a peptide bond between two amino acids is a condensation reaction because:
o: The two molecules simply add together
A molecule of water is eliminated
x: The –COOH of one amino acid reacts with the –NH₂ of another, losing H₂O and forming –CO–NH–. Joining with loss of a small molecule is condensation.

q: A single unbranched polypeptide chain contains 60 amino acid units. How many water molecules were eliminated in forming it?
x: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule, and a chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds. So 60 − 1 = 59 water molecules are eliminated.

q: The primary structure of a protein is:
o: The coiling of the chain into an α-helix
The sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
The folding of the chain into a three-dimensional shape
The association of several polypeptide chains
x: Primary structure is the order of amino acids, held by peptide bonds. Coiling is secondary, overall folding is tertiary, and the joining of several chains is quaternary structure.

q: The α-helix and β-pleated sheet of proteins are mainly held in shape by:
o: Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the peptide backbone
x: Secondary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide group and the N–H of another. Disulphide bridges and ionic attractions between side chains mainly hold the tertiary structure.

q: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to:
o: The order of amino acids in one chain
The local coiling of one chain
The arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains into one functional protein
The folding of one chain into a compact shape
x: Quaternary structure exists only in proteins made of more than one polypeptide chain. Haemoglobin, with four chains, is the standard example.

q: Which protein is a conjugated protein, carrying a non-protein (prosthetic) group?
x: Haemoglobin carries haem, an iron-containing prosthetic group, so it is a conjugated protein. Keratin, collagen and albumin are simple proteins made only of amino acids.

q: Which statement about globular proteins is correct?
o: They are long and thread-like and insoluble in water
They are made only of glycine units
They are folded into compact shapes and are usually soluble in water
x: Globular proteins, such as enzymes and haemoglobin, are folded into compact, roughly spherical shapes with polar groups outside, so they dissolve in water. Long, insoluble chains describe fibrous proteins.

q: Haemoglobin is classed as a conjugated protein because:
o: It contains a non-protein haem group attached to its polypeptide chains
It is formed by partial hydrolysis of another protein
It is made of a single polypeptide chain
x: A conjugated protein has a non-protein (prosthetic) group joined to the protein part. In haemoglobin this is haem, which contains iron. Simple proteins give only amino acids on hydrolysis.

q: When egg white is boiled, its protein is denatured. Which level of protein structure is NOT destroyed?
x: Heat breaks the weak hydrogen bonds and other attractions that hold the secondary and tertiary structure, so the protein unfolds and coagulates. The peptide bonds are not broken, so the amino acid sequence stays the same.

q: Two molecules of glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH (Mr = 75), join to form the dipeptide glycylglycine. Its relative molecular mass is (H₂O = 18):
x: Forming one peptide bond removes one water molecule: 2 × 75 − 18 = 132. 150 ignores the water lost, and 114 subtracts water twice.

q: The protein that carries oxygen in the blood is:
x: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen at the iron of its haem groups and releases it in the tissues. Keratin and collagen are structural proteins and casein is a milk protein.

q: Which protein is correctly matched with its role in the body?
x: Antibodies are proteins that bind foreign substances (antigens) and help the body fight infection. Keratin is structural, haemoglobin carries oxygen, and insulin is a hormone that lowers blood glucose.

q: The protein that gives strength to skin, tendons and bones is:
x: Collagen is a fibrous structural protein and the most abundant protein in the body, found in skin, tendons, cartilage and bone. The others are globular proteins with transport, hormone or other roles.

q: Essential amino acids are those that:
o: The body cannot make in sufficient amounts, so they must be obtained from food
Are found only in plant proteins
Contain sulphur in their side chain
x: The body can make some amino acids itself, but essential amino acids must come from dietary protein. A diet lacking any one of them limits the body's protein synthesis.

q: Kwashiorkor, seen in young children, is mainly caused by a diet lacking enough:
x: Kwashiorkor is a protein-deficiency disease, with swelling, poor growth and weak muscles. Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, lack of iodine causes goitre, and lack of iron causes anaemia.

q: The main nutritional importance of protein in the diet is to:
o: Act as the body's main long-term energy store
Provide most of the dietary fibre
Supply amino acids for growth and repair of tissues
x: Digested protein provides amino acids, which the body uses to build its own proteins for growth, repair, enzymes and hormones. Fat, not protein, is the main long-term energy store.

q: The proteins mainly responsible for muscle contraction are:
x: Actin and myosin are contractile proteins whose filaments slide over each other to shorten a muscle. Keratin and collagen are structural, and insulin and glucagon are hormones.

q: Casein, a phosphorus-containing protein of high nutritional value, is the main protein of:
x: Casein is the chief protein of milk and is a good source of essential amino acids. The main protein of egg white is albumin, and blood plasma contains albumins and globulins.

q: When equal masses of protein and fat are fully used for energy in the body:
o: Protein releases about twice as much energy as fat
Fat releases about twice as much energy as protein
Protein releases about four times as much energy as fat
x: Fat gives about 9 kcal per gram, while protein (like carbohydrate) gives about 4 kcal per gram. So fat gives a little over twice as much energy.

q: Chemically, most enzymes are:
x: Almost all enzymes are globular proteins, often with a non-protein cofactor or coenzyme. Their folded shape forms the active site where the substrate binds.

q: Enzymes increase the rate of a reaction by:
o: Lowering the activation energy by providing another pathway
Shifting the equilibrium towards the products
Raising the temperature of the reaction mixture
x: Like all catalysts, an enzyme provides a route with a lower activation energy, so more molecules can react. It speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally and does not change the equilibrium position.

q: When the temperature is raised well above the optimum for an enzyme, its activity falls because:
o: The enzyme is denatured and its active site loses its shape
The enzyme turns into a carbohydrate
x: High temperature breaks the weak bonds that hold the enzyme's three-dimensional shape. The active site no longer fits the substrate, so catalysis stops.

q: The enzyme urease catalyses the hydrolysis of urea, NH₂CONH₂. The products are:
x: NH₂CONH₂ + H₂O → 2NH₃ + CO₂, catalysed by urease. Urease was the first enzyme to be crystallised, which helped show that enzymes are proteins.

q: The enzyme zymase from yeast converts glucose into:
x: Zymase catalyses fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Splitting sucrose into glucose and fructose is done by invertase.

q: The enzyme invertase hydrolyses sucrose into:
x: Sucrose + H₂O → glucose + fructose, catalysed by invertase. Maltose gives two glucose units, and lactose gives glucose and galactose.

q: The high specificity of an enzyme for its substrate is explained by:
o: The enzyme being used up during the reaction
The enzyme raising the temperature at the active site
The lock-and-key model, in which the substrate fits the shape of the active site
The enzyme changing the products formed
x: Only a substrate whose shape and chemical groups match the active site can bind, just as only the right key fits a lock. This is why each enzyme catalyses one reaction or a small group of reactions.

q: The non-protein organic molecule that some enzymes need in order to work, often made from a vitamin, is called a:
x: A coenzyme is an organic cofactor, often derived from B vitamins, that binds to the enzyme and helps it act. The apoenzyme is the protein part alone, and a zymogen is an inactive enzyme precursor.

q: Which statement about an enzyme-catalysed reaction is correct?
o: The enzyme makes the reaction more exothermic
The enzyme is unchanged at the end and does not alter the position of equilibrium
The enzyme is used up in proportion to the product formed
The enzyme works equally well at all pH values
x: An enzyme is a catalyst: it is recovered unchanged and speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so ΔH and the equilibrium position stay the same. Enzymes have an optimum pH and lose activity away from it.

q: 180 g of glucose is completely fermented by zymase. The maximum mass of ethanol formed is (C 12, H 1, O 16):
x: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. 180 g is 1 mol of glucose, giving 2 mol ethanol = 2 × 46 = 92 g. 88 g is the mass of CO₂, and 46 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio.
